subtopic_detail: Nocturnal leg restlessness with a ferritin in the low normal range
stem:
A 52 year old woman attends your general practice with eighteen months of an unpleasant crawling sensation deep in both calves that comes on when she sits down in the evening and is worse when she goes to bed.

She describes an overwhelming need to move her legs, and says that walking around the house relieves it completely while she is moving. Her partner reports that she kicks in her sleep. She is exhausted during the day. She has no numbness, no weakness and no back pain, and her ankle reflexes and pedal pulses are normal. Her renal function and thyroid function are normal and she is not pregnant. She takes no antidepressant, antihistamine or antipsychotic.

data_table.Examination: Normal power, normal sensation to light touch and pinprick, ankle reflexes present, pedal pulses palpable, no varicosities
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 30 micrograms per litre (30-300), transferrin saturation 18 percent, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), creatinine 66 micromol/L (45-90), thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Symptom pattern: Onset at rest in the evening, relieved completely by movement, worse at night, partner reports periodic limb movements

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: Start pramipexole at a low dose and titrate to her symptoms
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists are effective but carry a substantial risk of augmentation, in which symptoms become earlier, more intense and more widespread over time, so they are no longer first line and are reserved for cases where iron repletion has failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start oral iron replacement and recheck her iron studies
options.rationale: Brain iron deficiency is the central mechanism in this condition, and iron replacement is recommended whenever the ferritin is at or below 75 micrograms per litre or the transferrin saturation is below 20 percent, even when these values fall within the standard laboratory reference range. Treating the iron first often resolves symptoms and avoids committing her to long term dopaminergic therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start pregabalin at night and review her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Alpha 2 delta ligands are a reasonable pharmacological option, particularly where pain is prominent, but they should follow correction of iron status rather than precede it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start a low dose benzodiazepine at night for the sleep disturbance
options.rationale: Sedatives may improve sleep continuity but do nothing for the sensory urge itself, and regular use in a chronic condition risks tolerance and dependence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Neurophysiology is indicated when examination suggests a peripheral neuropathy, but her sensation, power, reflexes and pulses are all normal and the history is characteristic, so testing would delay effective treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is a clinical diagnosis resting on an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, beginning or worsening at rest, relieved by movement, and worse in the evening or at night. Iron status is the first thing to assess and correct, because brain iron deficiency drives the disorder and the thresholds for treatment are higher than those used for anaemia: replacement is recommended at a ferritin of 75 micrograms per litre or below, or a transferrin saturation below 20 percent. This means a result reported as within the normal range still warrants treatment. Dopamine agonists, once standard, have fallen out of first line use because of augmentation, and alpha 2 delta ligands are generally preferred when drug treatment is needed.
key_points: Ferritin at or below 75 micrograms per litre is the treatment threshold, well above the anaemia threshold
Augmentation makes dopamine agonists a later line option than they once were
Review medications that provoke symptoms, including antidepressants, antihistamines and antipsychotics
Periodic limb movements in sleep frequently accompany the condition and support the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: A ferritin reported as normal is the commonest reason this condition goes untreated; read the actual number rather than the flag, because anything at or below 75 micrograms per litre is an indication for iron in a patient with these symptoms.

sources.label: Sleep Health Foundation: Restless legs syndrome

subtopic_detail: Cholestatic liver enzymes with a positive antimitochondrial antibody
stem:
A 54 year old woman attends your general practice with nine months of tiredness and itching that is worst at night and affects her whole body. She scratches until she bleeds and has not slept properly for months.

She drinks two standard drinks a week and takes no regular medication, herbal preparation or supplement. She has no jaundice, no abdominal pain and no pale stools or dark urine. Her alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamyl transferase are raised with only a mild rise in transaminases. An abdominal ultrasound shows a normal liver texture with no biliary dilatation and no gallstones. Antimitochondrial antibody is positive at a high titre and her immunoglobulin M is raised.

data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations, no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no xanthelasma, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L (30-110), gamma glutamyl transferase 310 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (less than 20), antimitochondrial antibody positive at high titre, immunoglobulin M raised, viral hepatitis serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Abdominal ultrasound shows normal liver texture, no biliary dilatation, no gallstones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start prednisolone and azathioprine and monitor her biochemistry
options.rationale: Immunosuppression is the treatment for autoimmune hepatitis, which produces a hepatitic rather than cholestatic pattern with high transaminases, positive smooth muscle or antinuclear antibodies and raised immunoglobulin G. It is ineffective here and adds steroid toxicity. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

options.text: Refer for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography urgently
options.rationale: Biliary intervention is directed at large duct obstruction, and her ultrasound shows no dilatation, so the procedure carries a risk of pancreatitis with no diagnostic or therapeutic yield. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and monitor her liver biochemistry
options.rationale: A cholestatic pattern with a high titre antimitochondrial antibody and normal biliary imaging in a middle aged woman is primary biliary cholangitis, and ursodeoxycholic acid is first line because it slows progression to cirrhosis and improves transplant free survival. Biochemical response at twelve months guides whether second line therapy is required. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

options.text: Start cholestyramine alone and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: A bile acid sequestrant is the first line treatment for the pruritus and should be offered, but symptom control alone leaves the underlying disease to progress towards cirrhosis. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

options.text: Arrange a liver biopsy before committing her to any drug treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is not required when the cholestatic biochemistry and antimitochondrial antibody are both present, and is reserved for atypical cases or suspected overlap with autoimmune hepatitis. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

explanation.summary: Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic autoimmune cholangiopathy that predominantly affects middle aged women and typically presents with fatigue and pruritus long before jaundice appears. The diagnosis can be made without biopsy when a cholestatic biochemical pattern is accompanied by a positive antimitochondrial antibody and imaging excludes large duct obstruction. Ursodeoxycholic acid is first line and improves transplant free survival, with response assessed biochemically at around twelve months and second line agents added for non responders. Pruritus is treated separately, usually beginning with a bile acid sequestrant, and patients need surveillance for osteoporosis, fat soluble vitamin deficiency and, once cirrhotic, for varices and hepatocellular carcinoma.
key_points: Cholestatic pattern plus antimitochondrial antibody plus normal ducts on imaging is sufficient for diagnosis
Ursodeoxycholic acid modifies disease; antipruritic therapy only treats the symptom
Biochemical response at twelve months determines the need for second line treatment
Screen for osteoporosis, because metabolic bone disease is a common and treatable complication
explanation.pearls: Separate cholestyramine from ursodeoxycholic acid by at least four hours: the sequestrant binds the therapeutic bile acid as readily as the ones causing the itch, and co administration quietly abolishes the benefit of the disease modifying drug.

subtopic_detail: Muscle aches with a moderately raised creatine kinase on a statin
stem:
A 61 year old man attends your general practice with six weeks of aching and heaviness in both thighs and shoulders that makes getting out of a low chair harder than it used to be. He started atorvastatin 40 mg daily four months ago after a myocardial infarction.

He has not changed his exercise, has done no unaccustomed heavy work and has not started any new medication, including no antifungal, macrolide or fibrate. He drinks minimal alcohol. His urine is normal in colour and his renal function is unchanged from baseline. He is worried because he has been told he must never stop the tablet after a heart attack.

data_table.Examination: Mild symmetrical proximal weakness of hip flexors and shoulder abductors, no rash, no muscle tenderness, reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 840 U/L (less than 200), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110) unchanged from baseline, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urinalysis negative for blood
data_table.Medication: Atorvastatin 40 mg daily for four months, aspirin, metoprolol, perindopril, no new interacting drug

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the statin dose and recheck his creatine kinase in two weeks
options.rationale: Dose reduction is a reasonable strategy for muscle symptoms with a normal or only mildly raised enzyme, but with a creatine kinase over four times the upper limit and objective proximal weakness the drug should be withheld entirely until the enzyme normalises. Continuing at any dose also leaves a reversible contributor unexamined. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Continue the statin unchanged and review his symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Continuing at full dose while the creatine kinase is over four times the upper limit with objective proximal weakness risks progression to rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Stop the statin permanently and record a statin allergy in his file
options.rationale: Labelling him permanently intolerant after one episode denies effective secondary prevention to a man who has had a myocardial infarction, when most patients tolerate rechallenge at a lower dose or with a different agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Withhold the statin and check his thyroid function before rechallenge
options.rationale: A creatine kinase between four and ten times the upper limit with proximal symptoms warrants temporary cessation, and hypothyroidism is a common and readily reversible contributor that must be excluded before the drug is blamed permanently. Once symptoms and enzymes normalise, rechallenge at a lower dose or with an alternative agent is appropriate because his cardiovascular indication is strong. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Add a fibrate to allow the statin dose to be reduced immediately
options.rationale: Combining a fibrate with a statin increases the risk of myopathy substantially, particularly with gemfibrozil, so it is the wrong direction in a patient who already has muscle symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Muscle symptoms are the commonest reason statins are stopped, and most are manageable without abandoning the drug. The creatine kinase level stratifies the response: symptoms with a normal or mildly raised enzyme can often be managed by dose reduction or a change of agent, a rise of four to ten times the upper limit warrants temporary cessation and investigation, and a rise above ten times or any evidence of rhabdomyolysis requires immediate cessation and assessment of renal function. Before attributing symptoms permanently to the statin, look for reversible contributors, particularly hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, interacting drugs and unaccustomed exertion. Rechallenge succeeds in most patients and matters because the secondary prevention benefit is large.
key_points: Check thyroid function before accepting a diagnosis of statin intolerance
Interacting drugs such as macrolides, azole antifungals and fibrates raise statin exposure
Persisting weakness with a very high creatine kinase after cessation raises immune mediated necrotising myopathy
Most patients tolerate rechallenge at a lower dose or with an alternative statin
explanation.pearls: If the creatine kinase keeps rising or the weakness persists weeks after stopping the drug, test for antibodies to 3 hydroxy 3 methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase: immune mediated necrotising myopathy does not resolve on withdrawal and needs immunosuppression rather than watchful waiting.
